title: Hold Expensive Cash So You Can Be the Buyer in a Crisis
documentTitle: Berkshire Hathaway Inc. — 2009 Annual Shareholder Letter
excerptForBlog:
Our gain in net worth during 2009 was $21.8 billion, which increased the per-share book value of both our Class A and Class B stock by 19.8%. Over the last 45 years (that is, since present management took over) book value has grown from $19 to $84,487, a rate of 20.3% compounded annually.

We will never become dependent on the kindness of strangers. Too-big-to-fail is not a fallback position at Berkshire. Instead, we will always arrange our affairs so that any requirements for cash we may conceivably have will be dwarfed by our own liquidity. Moreover, that liquidity will be constantly refreshed by a gusher of earnings from our many and diverse businesses. When the financial system went into cardiac arrest in September 2008, Berkshire was a supplier of liquidity and capital to the system, not a supplicant. At the very peak of the crisis, we poured $15.5 billion into a business world that could otherwise look only to the federal government for help. Of that, $9 billion went to bolster capital at three highly-regarded and previously-secure American businesses that needed — without delay — our tangible vote of confidence. The remaining $6.5 billion satisfied our commitment to help fund the purchase of Wrigley, a deal that was completed without pause while, elsewhere, panic reigned.

We pay a steep price to maintain our premier financial strength. The $20 billion-plus of cash-equivalent assets that we customarily hold is earning a pittance at present. But we sleep well.

lessonTitle: Hold Expensive Cash So You Can Be the Buyer in a Crisis
pullQuote: Liquidity is a strategic weapon disguised as a boring balance sheet item — its real return shows up only when everyone else runs out.
leadershipTraits: treats liquidity as a weapon, not a drag
willing to pay real costs for optionality
manages reputation as a deal-flow asset
situation: In March 2010, Warren Buffett filed Berkshire Hathaway's annual shareholder letter with the SEC, covering fiscal year 2009. The letter is addressed to shareholders and recaps a year that immediately followed the 2008 financial crisis. The core tension Buffett surfaces: Berkshire chose to hold $20 billion-plus in low-yield cash, a drag on returns, while making the case that this 'steep price' was worth paying.
insight:
The hidden move here is **deliberate optionality under stress**. Buffett draws a sharp line between companies that needed rescuing and Berkshire, which was 'a supplier of liquidity and capital to the system, not a supplicant.' At the peak of the crisis, Berkshire deployed $15.5 billion — including $9 billion into three named-but-unnamed 'highly-regarded' businesses and $6.5 billion into the Wrigley deal — precisely because it had the cash ready. That's the real return on idle money: the ability to act when competitors cannot.

This is a classic **competitive moat via financial structure**. Most companies optimize for current earnings, minimizing cash drag. Berkshire optimized for crisis capacity — and the 2008 freeze turned that 'costly' reserve into a $15.5 billion deal flow advantage. The letter even names the mechanism: liquidity 'constantly refreshed by a gusher of earnings from our many and diverse businesses.' The cash pile isn't static savings; it's backed by recurring cash generation, which makes holding it sustainable.
application: Map your own liquidity position against a specific bad scenario: what happens if revenue drops 40% for six months? If you'd be calling investors for help, you're a supplicant. Build a cash reserve sized to that scenario — even if it earns nothing — and treat it as the entry fee for being a buyer when your market next freezes.
